name: Catalysis and catalyst theory
note: The kernel: some substances accelerate reaction without participating in it. This explains why platinum speeds many reactions and why heated iron catalyses ammonia decomposition. You cannot build a contact process or ammonia synthesis without understanding this.

name: High-pressure autoclave and steam digester
note: High pressure demands absolute rigidity and control. The drum must withstand internal stress while keeping temperature uniform. Failures are catastrophic. The riveted seams are the critical weak point; you need sub-millimetre alignment and reliable riveting technique.

name: Bourdon tube pressure gauge and safety relief valve
note: The Bourdon tube uncurls proportionally to pressure, moving a needle on a dial. The relief valve must crack at exactly the safe pressure or the autoclave becomes a bomb. Precision here saves lives.

name: Contact process for sulfuric acid using platinum catalyst
note: Platinum refuses to poison and remains active indefinitely. The trick: SO2 feed purity above 99.5% or the catalyst silts up. Temperature control to 400-450 C is critical - too hot and equilibrium shifts wrong, too cool and kinetics stall. This yields acid with 98% sulfur recovery, halving the cost versus lead chamber.

name: Vanadium pentoxide catalyst for contact sulfuric acid
note: Vanadium catalyst poisons slowly from trace impurities in SO2 feed, requiring periodic regeneration, but costs one-twentieth of platinum. The silica support geometry matters: small pellets expose more surface but choke flow; large pellets flow freely but starve for area. Industrial practice settles on 3-5mm rings.

name: Oleum (fuming sulfuric acid) production
note: Oleum contains free SO3 dissolved in H2SO4. It is phenomenally corrosive and must be stored in glass-lined steel or lead, never iron. Used for nitration of aromatics where ordinary sulfuric acid is too dilute. The hazard is water contact - violently exothermic absorption of moisture releases heat that can vaporize the whole batch.

name: Solvay process: ammonia-soda manufacturing
output_unbounded_reason: its product is priced at the dearer incumbent route, so a derived payback falls under the floor (Complaints/329)
note: The genius: ammonia is expensive so you recycle it. Limestone calcines to CO2 which carbonates the ammonia-brine. NaHCO3 precipitates, is filtered, then thermally decomposed to soda ash. The ammonia is recovered by treating the residue with lime and distilling. Leblanc loses all this to slag mountains. Solvay's yield is 80% versus Leblanc's 40%, and the only waste is calcium chloride brines.

name: Ammonia recovery and regeneration in soda plants
note: The Solvay cycle is only better than Leblanc if you actually recover the ammonia. This requires distilling the mother liquor under controlled heat and condensing the vapour in a coil condenser. Without ammonia recycling, Solvay is just another expensive acid-soda process.

name: Deacon process: oxidation of hydrogen chloride to chlorine
note: Converts otherwise-waste HCl from nitrification into chlorine gas. The copper chloride catalyst cycles between Cu(II) oxide and Cu(I) chloride. Temperature above 1600 C is critical; below that, conversion drops sharply. Heat recovery from the exothermic reaction is essential to the economics.

name: Weldon process: regeneration of manganese dioxide from manganous chloride
note: In bleach production, MnO2 is reduced to MnCl2. Weldon's trick: oxidise the manganese back with hypochlorite, then filter and recycle the MnO2. This more than halves manganese consumption. Lime is needed to adjust pH so precipitation is quantitative.

name: Bleaching powder: mixed calcium hypochlorite
annual_output_basis: A bleach works of about twelve hands working two thousand hours a year each at the seventy-five hours a tonne the entry states: roughly three hundred tonnes of powder. Declared plant size from the entry's own hours, conf C.
note: Chlorine dissolves directly into lime slurry. The product is a mixture of Ca(OCl)2, CaCl2, and excess lime that is chemically stable and safe to handle dry. It became the standard bleach for cloth and later drinking water because chlorine gas is too corrosive and dangerous to transport.

name: Chlor-alkali process: mercury cathode cell
note: Mercury wets the cathode, preventing hydrogen evolution and protecting sodium metal that would otherwise form. Sodium amalgamates into the mercury, is drawn off and reacted with water to yield NaOH. This yields caustic soda of exceptional purity, but mercury is volatile and extremely toxic. Worker exposure to mercury vapour causes tremor, gingivitis and permanent neurological damage. The process dominates industry for fifty years but is eventually abandoned because of environmental and health costs.

name: Chlor-alkali process: asbestos diaphragm cell
note: Asbestos diaphragm avoids mercury entirely. Chlorine is produced at the anode, hydrogen at the cathode. The diaphragm prevents mixing while allowing ions to pass. Caustic product is dilute (5-10%) so requires concentration by evaporation. Eventually diaphragm cells replace mercury because the health cost of mercury is unsustainable, but asbestos dust also kills workers decades later.

name: Caustic soda: concentration and purification
output_unbounded_reason: one declared total would be split across unrelated products, so no single output bounds it
note: Caustic soda boils above 100 C, so direct heating to dryness would decompose it. Vacuum evaporation keeps temperature below 100 C while removing water. The product is chemically pure but must be handled in glass or lead; iron is attacked immediately and dissolved.

name: Ostwald process: oxidation of ammonia to nitric acid
note: Platinum gauze at 800-900 C oxidises ammonia to nitrogen oxides in seconds. The nitrogen oxides are then absorbed in water to yield nitric acid. This is cheaper than the saltpetre-based or lead chamber methods and yields pure dilute acid. Platinum is essential; iron corrodes instantly under these conditions.

name: Haber-Bosch synthesis of ammonia
note: At atmospheric pressure, ammonia synthesis requires 1000 C to reach useful conversion. At 200 atmospheres, equilibrium shifts right so that 400-500 C gives industrial conversion. The iron catalyst works because iron nitride acts as an intermediate, regenerating quickly. Regenerative heat exchange between inlet and outlet gases is mandatory to keep the furnace economical. One plant feeds the entire world's fertiliser supply.

name: Cyanamide process: nitrogen fixation by carbide
note: Calcium carbide is made by arc furnace: limestone and coke to 3000 C in one step. The carbide then reacts with nitrogen gas at 1000 C to yield calcium cyanamide, which hydrolyses to ammonia. This route predates Haber-Bosch and requires less pressure, but yields fewer tonnes per unit energy. Arc furnace demands kilowatts of electric power.

name: Electric arc nitrogen fixation: nitrogen oxides from air
note: The arc-furnace method is energy-intensive but simple. At 3000 C, nitrogen and oxygen in air briefly combine to NO, which is then absorbed in water and oxidised to HNO3. This was the first synthetic method and remains a fallback when electricity is cheap. It yields only 2-3% conversion per pass, so most gas is unreacted.

name: Superphosphate: acidulation of rock phosphate
output_unbounded_reason: the line's basis unit is not a kilogram, so a declared annual_output_t cannot bound it
note: Rock phosphate is insoluble calcium phosphate. Sulfuric acid converts it to a mixture of soluble monocalcium phosphate and gypsum. The product is simply filtered and dried. This produces tens of tonnes of agricultural fertiliser from a tonne of sulfuric acid. The phosphate is now bioavailable to plants.

note: Potash salts like sylvinite are mined like any mineral ore. The mined rock is then dissolved in water, filtered to remove insoluble matter, and crystallised. Potassium is essential to agriculture: wheat and potatoes are heavy exporters of K2O, depleting soils rapidly without replenishment.

name: Coal tar fractionation and distillation
note: Coal tar boiling below 300 C contains benzene, toluene, phenol. Above 300 C come naphthalene and anthracene. Fractional distillation with bubble-cap trays gives cuts of surprising purity if reflux is high. The vapour pressure differences are only a factor of two, so reflux ratio must exceed 10:1 to separate them properly.

name: Fractionating column with bubble caps
note: Bubble caps are short tubes with caps, welded into copper trays so vapour must bubble through liquid, creating intimate contact. At each tray, liquid and vapour come to partial equilibrium. Boiling point differences of just 10 C become separable if you run fifty trays with high reflux. This is the workhorse of the petrochemical industry.

name: Benzene extraction from coal tar
note: Benzene boils at 80 C, well separated from toluene at 111 C. A fractionating column with 20-30 trays yields benzene at 99% purity. Benzene vapour is intensely toxic; chronic exposure causes aplastic anaemia. Early workers in benzene manufacturing died of leukaemia within a few years of exposure.

name: Aniline from benzene via nitrobenzene
note: Oleum nitrates benzene to nitrobenzene in minutes. Reduction with iron powder in dilute acid yields aniline. Aniline is a colourless liquid, bp 184 C, that polymerises in air to a black tar unless kept dry. It is the keystone of synthetic dyes and must be kept under nitrogen or mineral oil.

name: Azo dyes: diazotisation and azo coupling
note: Aniline plus nitrous acid yields ArN2+ diazonium salt. This is weakly stable in acid at 0 C and couples to nucleophilic aromatics yielding azo dyes with colours from bright red to deep black. Azo dyes are wash-fast because the ArN=NAr group is chemically stable. Millions of tonnes are made industrially each year.

name: Alizarin synthesis: oxidation of anthraquinone
note: Anthraquinone is easily extracted from coal tar. Oxidation with air and catalysts yields alizarin. Before synthesis, alizarin dye came from madder root cultivation in fields, so synthetic alizarin crashed the price by 99%, destroying the madder industry. This is the first wholly synthetic industrial organic dye and set the pattern for the twentieth century.

name: Indigo synthesis from N-phenylglycine
note: Synthetic indigo is prepared by alkali fusion of a glycine-aniline intermediate at exactly 180 C. Unlike alizarin, indigo is sparingly soluble in water so it is used by converting to the reduced leuco base. When synthetic indigo was commercialised in 1897, indigo-dyeing agriculture in India and West Indies collapsed. Millions of farmers lost their livelihood. This is the first and most politically consequential chemical synthesis.

name: Saccharin synthesis
note: Toluene is sulfonated with oleum, giving toluenesulfonic acid. Oxidation with permanganate to toluic acid, then reaction with ammonia and loss of water yields saccharin. Saccharin is 500 times sweeter than sugar by mass and costs one-tenth as much at scale. Food preservation becomes possible without cane sugar.

name: Salicylic acid: hydroxylation of benzenesulfonic acid
note: Benzene is sulfonated to benzenesulfonic acid. Molten alkali at 300 C causes Ar-SO3H to be replaced by Ar-OH, yielding phenol. Phenol is then converted to salicylic acid. Salicylic acid is acetylated to yield aspirin, the world's most widely used pharmaceutical.

name: Aspirin synthesis from salicylic acid
note: Salicylic acid tastes bitter and upsets the stomach. Acetylation to aspirin does not reduce the anti-inflammatory effect but eliminates most gastrointestinal irritation. Aspirin revolutionises medicine; mass manufacture becomes possible after the synthesis chain is optimised.

name: Sulfonamide antibiotics: sulfanilamide synthesis
note: Sulfanilamide (para-aminobenzenesulfonamide) is synthesised by sulfonation of aniline followed by reaction with ammonia. It inhibits bacterial dihydropteroate synthase, blocking folate metabolism. Sulfonamides are the first fully synthetic antibiotics and are miraculous compared to no antibiotics at all, though they have significant toxicity.

name: Continuous versus batch processing decision
note: Continuous reactors have lower capital cost per tonne when scale is large and products are stable. Batch processes suit pharmaceutical work where recipes change frequently and product shelf-life is measured in months. Continuous operation demands process control; any upset propagates downstream.

name: Corrosion-resistant plant: lead and lead-lined vessels
note: Sulfuric acid dissolves iron instantly but is nearly inert to lead. The acid tank is lined with lead sheet, joined by soft-solder, and sealed with a lead gasket. Lead is soft, so it is cast thick to resist rupture from external mechanical stress. This was the standard until stainless steel displaced it in the 1950s.

name: Corrosion-resistant vessels: acid-resistant stoneware
note: High-fired stoneware has sufficient mechanical strength for small vessels and is inert to all acids. The glaze must be ash-based or lead-based and fully matured. Stoneware is cheaper than lead but brittle, so it is used for containers and small reaction vessels up to ten litres. Industrial-scale acid storage still required lead-lined iron.

name: Glass-lined steel vessels
note: Glass fuses to steel at 1400 C. The thermal expansion mismatch between glass and steel causes peeling if temperature gradients are steep. Industrial practice uses special borosilicate glasses and slow heating and cooling. Glass-lined vessels combine steel strength with glass's chemical resistance.

name: Stainless steel vessels for corrosive service
note: Chromium above 13% in steel passivates the surface, preventing corrosion. Nickel is added for chloride resistance. 304 stainless is austenitic and weldable. Costs three times as much as carbon steel but outlasts it by an order of magnitude in corrosive service. Stainless steel eventually became the material of choice for all chemical plant.

name: Filter press: plate-and-frame filtration
note: Slurry is pumped into the space between cloth-lined plates, then pressure forces liquid through cloth while solids accumulate. When blocked, plates are separated and solids are knocked out. This is tedious but effective at achieving 1-2 micron clarity. Continuous filter designs exist but are slower.

name: Industrial centrifuge for separation
note: A scroll inside a spinning cylinder conveys sediment toward the outlet while supernatant overflows a weir. Centrifugal force is 1000 times gravity, so settling that would take hours happens in minutes. Bearing wear from the immense centrifugal force is the main maintenance burden.

name: Surface evaporator for concentration
note: Copper or iron tubes are immersed in the liquid to be concentrated and steam is passed through them. Boiling point elevation means the solution boils above 100 C at higher concentration; temperature control is critical to avoid bumping and foaming.

name: Crystallisation and crystal separation
note: Cooling a saturated solution nucleates crystals that grow if undisturbed. Temperature control to within 1 C is essential. Impurities prefer to stay dissolved, so crystals are purer than the starting solution. This is the principal method of refining all salts.

name: Ion exchange resins for water softening and purification
note: Phenolic or acrylic polymer beads are cross-linked with divinylbenzene and charged with either H+ cations or OH- anions. Water percolated through the column exchanges Ca2+ for H+, softening and acidifying simultaneously. The resin is regenerated with acid or base. Ion exchange is essential for producing ultrapure process water and boiler feedwater.

name: Chromatography: column and paper methods
note: A solution of mixed compounds is percolated through a column of silica gel or charcoal. Compounds with different affinities for the stationary phase elute separately. Paper chromatography using capillary action works in smaller scales and requires only filter paper and solvent.

name: Electroplating: deposition of nickel, chromium and precious metals
kb: Electrodeposition of metal ions onto a cathode to coat an object
note: The object to be coated is the cathode. Current density must be controlled; too high and the deposit is burnt and powdery, too low and adhesion suffers. Electroplating of chromium requires three stages: copper strike, nickel, then thin chromium for corrosion resistance.

name: Leblanc process waste: calcium carbide and the alkali waste problem
note: One tonne of soda ash from Leblanc produces three tonnes of toxic sulfide waste. Dumping it into rivers creates hydrogen sulfide gas and kills fisheries. Britain's Alkali Act of 1863 was the first environmental regulation in history, requiring soda makers to absorb 95% of the acid mist. This made Leblanc uneconomical where Solvay could operate.

name: Industrial hygiene and occupational chemical poisoning
note: Phosphorus necrosis (phossy jaw) comes from white phosphorus dust eroding jaw bone. Mercury causes tremor and neurological damage. Lead accumulates in bone and poisons the nervous system. Benzene vapour causes aplastic anaemia. Chlorine gas causes pulmonary oedema. No safe level exists; only elimination of exposure through ventilation and process redesign stops the poisoning.

name: Dynamite: nitroglycerin in diatomaceous earth
note: Nitroglycerin soaks into diatomaceous earth, rendering it safe from accidental detonation during handling but equally detonatable by blasting cap. This makes large-scale mining and construction possible. The name dynamite became synonymous with Nobel's wealth and the peace prize.

name: TNT: trinitrotoluene synthesis

note: Phenol is nitrated to yield a yellow acid that is surprisingly stable. Picric acid is used as a dye and in photoflash powder. Its use as a military explosive faded when TNT became available because TNT is more powerful and much less hygroscopic.

name: Blasting cap and fulminate detonator
note: A blasting cap is useless without an initiator: a tiny shock-sensitive charge inside. Mercury fulminate explodes from spark, friction or impact. The detonator shock wave initiates the main explosive charge. Without the detonator, TNT and dynamite are inert. The detonator is what makes high explosives strategically useful.

note: Mercury is dissolved in dilute nitric acid and ethanol added. After a few hours, white crystals of mercury fulminate form. These are highly shock-sensitive and explode from any mechanical disturbance. Synthesis must be done in tiny batches and handled with extreme caution. Lead fulminate is safer but less reliable.

name: Casein plastics from milk protein
note: Milk is acidified to precipitate casein protein. The wet casein is dried and mixed with formaldehyde, then heated and moulded. The product is hard, waterproof, and can be dyed. Casein plastic was used for buttons, fountain pens, and jewellery until phenolic plastics displaced it.

name: Bakelite: phenol-formaldehyde plastic
note: Phenol and formaldehyde condense at 150-180 C in the presence of acid catalyst. The resin is thermoset: once cured, it cannot be remelted. Bakelite is hard, brittle, and heat-resistant. It is used for electrical insulation, radio bodies, and industrial equipment. It was the first fully synthetic plastic and dominated the 1920s.

name: Polyvinyl chloride (PVC) synthesis
kb: Polymerisation of vinyl chloride monomer under free-radical initiation

Plasticisers are added to make flexible sheet; unplasticised PVC is rigid and chemical-resistant. PVC is the most widely used plastic on Earth. Thermal decomposition releases hydrogen chloride, making fires extremely dangerous.

name: Nylon 6,6 synthesis and polymerisation
note: Adipic acid is made by oxidising cyclohexane with HNO3. Hexamethylenediamine comes from adiponitrile and ammonia. These are condensed at 250 C under controlled pressure, forming long polyamide chains. Nylon has a melting point of 265 C and can be drawn to strong fibres. Nylon is the first fully synthetic fibre and is used for everything from stockings to parachutes.

name: Silver halide photographic chemistry
kb: Sensitisation of silver halide emulsions and development chemistry for silver images
note: Silver halide crystals are formed by mixing silver nitrate and sodium halide. Gelatin is added as a binder. Development is performed with reducing agents like hydroquinone or metol in alkaline conditions. Each step requires strict control of temperature, pH and oxidising impurities. Photographic film is the foundation of cinema and still photography.

name: Ammonia as refrigerant in compression cycles
note: Ammonia has a high latent heat and boils at -33 C. Liquid ammonia evaporates in the cold box and is compressed back to liquid, rejecting heat in the condenser. Ammonia is toxic and requires sealed copper tubing, but it is non-reactive with copper and iron. Industrial food freezing and ice manufacturing rely on ammonia refrigeration.

name: Toluene extraction from coal tar
note: Toluene boils at 111 C, well separated from benzene at 80 C. A fractionating column yields toluene at 99% purity. Toluene is used as a solvent and as a precursor to TNT and saccharin. It is less toxic than benzene but still a CNS depressant at high vapour concentrations.

name: Phenol extraction from coal tar and synthesis
annual_output_basis: One tar-distillery fractionating the tar of a large gasworks or coke-oven battery; phenols are a few tenths of a percent of the tar, giving the order of five hundred tonnes of phenol a year. Declared plant size, conf C.
note: Coal tar contains phenol in the middle boiling fraction. Early sources used distillation. Later, benzene is sulfonated and the sulfonate is fused with molten alkali at 300 C to yield phenol. Phenol is corrosive to skin, denatures proteins and was the first antiseptic used by Lister.

name: Naphthalene extraction and purification
note: Naphthalene boils at 218 C and crystallises easily. Multiple crystallisation cycles yield pure white needles. Naphthalene is used as a mothball, as a precursor to phthalic anhydride for plasticisers, and in dye synthesis. Its toxicity is low but volatility is significant in enclosed spaces.

name: Anthracene extraction and oxidation
note: Anthracene is the highest boiling component of coal tar. It crystallises readily and is extremely pure after recrystallisation. Oxidation of anthracene yields anthraquinone, which is further oxidised to alizarin. Anthracene is also photosensitive and used in photochemistry.

name: Activated carbon production and use
note: Charcoal is heated with steam at 900 C. Water reacts with carbon, gasifying the interior and creating a porous structure with enormous surface area, up to 3000 m2/g. Activated carbon adsorbs colour, odour and trace contaminants. It is used for water treatment and gas purification. Steam is not a stocked material - it is water raised on the spot by the same furnace this node already burns coal_kg for, and pricing it as a separate purchased kilogram double-counted the fuel. Folded into coal_kg instead: 100 kg of steam needs roughly 2.6 MJ/kg to heat feedwater from ambient to boiling and then vaporise it (sensible heat plus the ~2.26 MJ/kg latent heat of vaporisation this file's own brine-boiling entries use), which at a rough 20 percent furnace efficiency (matching lime_kg's kiln estimate in data/production/30_fuel_stone.json, since this is the same kind of furnace-integrated boiler rather than an insulated one built for the purpose) and coal's ~29 MJ/kg calorific value comes to about 45 kg of coal - 200 kg for the activation reaction itself plus that 45 kg for the steam, giving 245 kg total. The req_any steam_supply group below already gates this node on having SOME steam-generating technology; that answers whether you can raise steam at all, which is a different question from how much fuel this one batch burns doing it, so both stay.

name: Water treatment by coagulation and settling
note: Fine clay and organic particles remain suspended in water as colloids. Alum or ferric sulfate ions hydrolyse to form hydroxide gelatine that neutralises colloid charges. Particles flocculate and settle quickly. This is the first step in modern water purification.

name: Sand filtration and multimedia filter beds
note: After coagulation, water passes through a filter bed of coarse gravel, sand, and sometimes anthracite coal. The bed removes particles down to 10 microns. The filter must be backwashed periodically when pressure drop becomes excessive.

name: Chlorination of drinking water for disinfection
note: Chlorine kills bacteria within seconds at concentrations above 0.2 ppm. Residual chlorine must be maintained to prevent recontamination in pipes. Chlorination remains the standard method for microbiological control of water supplies.

name: Formaldehyde oxidation of methanol
note: Methanol vapour is oxidised over silver gauze at 600 C. Formaldehyde is produced as an equilibrium mixture with methanol and water; the product is stabilised by dissolving in water as formalin. Formaldehyde is a cross-linking reagent for proteins and cellulose, essential for resins.

name: White phosphorus extraction from bone ash
annual_output_basis: A match-industry works with one or two retorts reducing bone-ash phosphate, about one tonne of phosphorus a week over fifty weeks. Declared plant size, conf C.
note: Bone ash is calcined phosphate. Heating with carbon in a closed retort at 1300 C reduces it to phosphorus vapour. The vapour is condensed under water to white phosphorus. This method dates to 1669 and predates the identification of phosphorus as an element by 100 years.
